name: Person Perception and Attributions
what: This subtopic examines how we form mental impressions of other people and how we decide what caused their behaviour. It covers direct and indirect perception, first impressions, and the three-step cognitive process of attribution.
why: Understanding how we perceive and judge others helps explain why interpersonal conflicts arise, why we sometimes misjudge people, and how our social decisions are shaped by mental shortcuts rather than objective facts.

items.title: I can define person perception and distinguish between direct and indirect sources of information
items.what: Person perception refers to the mental processes used to understand and form impressions of others. Information can come directly from the person through observation or interaction, or indirectly through a third party such as a friend's description or an online profile.
items.why: Recognising the source of our impressions helps us assess their reliability. Indirect information is filtered through another person's interpretation and may be less accurate than direct observation.
items.example: You observe a classmate sleeping in class (direct perception). Later, a friend tells you that classmate is lazy and unmotivated (indirect perception). Your final impression is shaped by both sources, but the indirect source may be biased.

items.title: I can explain what a first impression is and describe its influence on decision-making and interpersonal interactions
items.what: A first impression is a snap judgement formed within less than a second of meeting someone, based on easily accessible surface information such as appearance and body language. These impressions can persist and influence later behaviour toward that person.
items.why: First impressions affect who we choose to interact with, whether we offer someone a job, and how much trust we extend to a stranger. Understanding their influence helps explain why initial judgements can be unfair and hard to revise.
items.example: A job interviewer immediately forms a positive impression of a candidate who makes eye contact, sits upright, and is dressed formally. This first impression influences the interviewer's decision to shortlist the candidate before asking a single question.

items.title: I can outline the three steps in the cognitive process of attribution
items.what: Attribution involves three ordered steps: first, observing a behaviour; second, consciously acknowledging what the behaviour was; and third, deciding on a cause for that behaviour. This process occurs constantly as we try to make sense of the actions of people around us.
items.why: Understanding the steps in attribution clarifies that the judgements we make about causes are interpretive, not factual. At step three, different people can assign very different causes to the exact same observed behaviour.
items.example: You see a student yelling in a corridor (step 1). You register that they are shouting angrily (step 2). You conclude they must be aggressive or rude by nature (step 3), even though they may have just received very bad news.

items.title: I can distinguish between internal and external attributions and provide examples of each
items.what: Internal (personal) attributions assign the cause of behaviour to something within the individual, such as their personality, ability, or motivation. External (situational) attributions assign the cause to factors outside the individual, such as the environment, circumstances, or other people's actions.
items.why: The type of attribution made has real consequences for how we treat others and how we respond to our own failures or successes. Internal attributions can lead to blame, while external attributions can foster empathy.
items.example: A colleague arrives late to a meeting. An internal attribution: they are disorganised and don't value others' time. An external attribution: there was an unexpected road closure on their route. The same behaviour receives a fundamentally different explanation.

items.title: I can define the fundamental attribution error and explain why it occurs
items.what: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to explain other people's behaviour using internal factors while overlooking possible external causes. It arises because when observing someone else, the person themselves is the most visually salient feature, not the situation they are in.
items.why: This error is one of the most common sources of misjudgement in social life. It can cause us to unfairly blame individuals for circumstances largely beyond their control, affecting both personal relationships and professional settings.
items.example: A shopper snaps at a cashier. An observer attributes this to the shopper being a rude and unkind person (internal), ignoring the possibility that the shopper just received devastating news about a family member (external).

items.title: I can describe what an attributional style is and explain how it can influence future behaviour
items.what: Attributional style refers to the consistent pattern in the types of attributions a person tends to make. Someone who habitually attributes failure to stable internal factors, such as believing they are simply bad at something, may develop learned helplessness and stop trying to improve.
items.why: Research in educational psychology shows that students who attribute failure to changeable internal causes, such as insufficient effort, are more likely to improve than those who attribute it to fixed causes. Recognising one's own attributional style can be a tool for personal development.
items.example: A student who fails a chemistry test and thinks 'I am just not a science person and never will be' has a pessimistic, stable attributional style. A student who thinks 'I did not study the right sections this time' has an unstable internal attribution and is more likely to change their approach.
